title: Small talk
grammar: Small words that set the tone: maar, even, eens, toch, wel, hoor
summary: Unstressed little words in the middle of the sentence set the tone: even and eens make a request light, maar gives permission, toch asks for agreement, wel contradicts or reassures, hoor at the end is friendly.
explain:
Dutch speakers colour almost every sentence with small unstressed words: *modal particles* (de modale partikels). They do not change the facts, they change the tone: friendly, impatient, reassuring, surprised. Without them Dutch sounds abrupt. `Wacht!` is an order; `Wacht even` is a friendly 'just a moment'. They have no direct English translation, so learn them as tones.

### Making a request friendly: even, eens, maar

| word | what it adds | example |
| even | only a moment, no big deal | Kun je even helpen? |
| eens | a friendly push or invitation | Kijk eens! |
| maar | go ahead, you may | Ga maar zitten. |

> Mag ik je even iets vragen? — Can I ask you something?
> Kom eens langs. — Come round some time.
> Zeg het maar. — Go ahead, tell me. / What can I get you?

- `maar` also means **only**: `Ik heb maar vijf euro`. With `niet` it means *better not*: `Doe dat maar niet`.
- `eens` also means *some time*: `Ik wil eens naar Japan`. And `niet eens` is *not even*.
- Stressed `even` is a different word: `even groot` (just as big).

### toch

- **Asking for agreement**: `Je komt toch?` (You are coming, aren't you?). It can also stand at the end: `Je komt, toch?`
- **Surprise or a reproach**: `Dat weet je toch?` (Surely you know that?)
- **Insisting**: `Kom toch binnen!` (Do come in!)
- **Anyway, after all**, stressed: `Ik ga toch` (I am going anyway).

### wel

- **Contradicting a negative**: `Hij komt niet. — Hij komt wel!` To say yes to a negative question, use `jawel`, not just `ja`.
- **Reassuring**: `Het komt wel goed` (It will be all right).
- **Probably**, with `zullen`: `Hij zal wel ziek zijn`.
- **Granted …, but**: `Dat klopt wel, maar …`

### hoor

`hoor` goes at the **end** of a statement, or straight after `ja` and `nee`. It is friendly and takes the edge off: `Ja hoor`, `Nee hoor`, `Dat is niet erg, hoor`. It **never** goes in a question, and it does not belong in formal writing.

### nou, gewoon, zeker, dan

- `nou` (the spoken form of `nu`) starts a reaction, `Nou, ik weet het niet`, or adds impatience: `Kom nou!`
- `gewoon`: just, simply, without fuss: `Zeg het gewoon`.
- `zeker`, unstressed, makes a guess you want confirmed: `Je bent zeker moe?` (I suppose you are tired?)
- `dan` in a question reacts to what the other person just said: `Wat is er dan?` `Waarom dan?`

> Je bent zeker de nieuwe collega? — I suppose you are the new colleague?
> Wat is er dan? — What is the matter, then?

### Where they go

Particles stand in the middle of the sentence: after the verb and the subject, **after** short pronouns such as `het`, `me`, `je`, `hem`, and **before** `niet` and the verbs at the end.

> Kun je me even helpen? — Can you help me for a moment?
> Doe het toch maar niet. — Better not do it after all.

A noun object with `de` or `het` can stand on either side: `Geef me even het zout` and `Geef me het zout even` are both fine. When particles pile up, the order is fixed: `dan` / `nou`, `toch`, `maar`, `eens`, `even`. `Kom dan toch maar eens even langs` is a famous example, but one or two at a time is normal.

### Watch out

- No hoor in a question: *Kunt u me helpen, hoor? → `Kunt u me even helpen?`
- A pronoun comes before the particle: *Zeg maar het → `Zeg het maar`; *Kun je even me helpen? → `Kun je me even helpen?`
- `maar` in the middle is not *but*: `Ga maar` means *go ahead*.
- Contradict a negative with `wel`, not with `ja`: `Ben je niet moe? — Jawel.`

### Compared with Ukrainian

Ukrainian has similar little words, such as `ж` (`Ти ж прийдеш?` — `Je komt toch?`) and `-но` (`Подивись-но!` — `Kijk eens!`), but they do not match the Dutch ones one to one.

words.en: to be right / to be correct

sentences.nl: Sorry, stoor ik even? Ik heb een korte vraag.
sentences.en: Sorry, am I disturbing you for a moment? I have a quick question.
sentences.note: Even makes the interruption small: only a moment. Without it, Stoor ik? sounds heavier.

sentences.nl: Ga maar zitten, ik zet even koffie.
sentences.en: Go ahead and sit down, I'll just make some coffee.
sentences.note: Maar in an order gives permission or encouragement: go ahead. Even makes the coffee-making a small, quick thing.
alt: Ga maar zitten, dan zet ik even koffie.

sentences.nl: Kom trouwens eens langs, dan kunnen we gezellig kletsen.
sentences.en: By the way, come round some time, then we can have a nice chat.
sentences.note: Eens turns the order into a friendly invitation. It stands in the middle, before the separable part langs at the end.
alt: Trouwens, kom eens langs, dan kunnen we gezellig kletsen.

sentences.nl: Je komt toch ook naar het feest?
sentences.en: You are coming to the party too, aren't you?
sentences.note: Toch asks the other person to agree, like an English tag question. It stands right after the verb and the subject.
alt: Jij komt toch ook naar het feest?
Je komt ook naar het feest, toch?
Jij komt ook naar het feest, toch?

sentences.nl: Dat klopt wel, maar je overdrijft een beetje.
sentences.en: That is true enough, but you are exaggerating a bit.
sentences.note: Wel … maar grants one point and then adds an objection. Here maar is the ordinary 'but', joining two sentences.
alt: Dat klopt wel, maar jij overdrijft een beetje.

sentences.nl: Hij is er nog niet. Hij zal wel in de file staan.
sentences.en: He is not here yet. He is probably stuck in a traffic jam.
sentences.note: Zal … wel is a guess: probably. The speaker does not know, but thinks it likely.

sentences.nl: Dat maakt helemaal niet uit, hoor.
sentences.en: That doesn't matter at all, honestly.
sentences.note: Hoor at the end makes the reassurance warm and friendly. It is only used at the end of a statement, never in a question.

sentences.nl: Ik kan maar even blijven, want ik moet nog koken.
sentences.en: I can only stay for a little while, because I still have to cook.
sentences.note: Here maar means 'only', and even means 'a short time'. Together, maar even: only briefly.

sentences.nl: Wat bedoel je dan met die opmerking?
sentences.en: What do you mean by that remark, then?
sentences.note: Dan in a question reacts to what the other person has just said. It stands after the verb and the subject.
alt: Wat bedoel jij dan met die opmerking?

sentences.nl: Je bent zeker de nieuwe collega?
sentences.en: I suppose you are the new colleague?
sentences.note: Unstressed zeker in a statement with a question mark is a guess you want confirmed. It does not mean 'certainly' here.
alt: Jij bent zeker de nieuwe collega?

exercises.nl: Mag ik je ___ onderbreken? Ik heb een vraag.
exercises.en: May I interrupt you for a moment? I have a question.
exercises.note: Even makes the request small and polite. Hoor never goes in a question, and zeker would make it a guess.

exercises.nl: Mag ik hier zitten? — Ja hoor, ga ___ zitten.
exercises.en: May I sit here? — Of course, go ahead and sit down.
exercises.note: Maar gives permission: go ahead. Eens would be your own suggestion, not an answer to a request, and wel contradicts a negative.

exercises.nl: Eerlijk gezegd vind ik die film niet zo goed. — Nou, ik vind hem ___ goed!
exercises.en: To be honest I don't think that film is very good. — Well, I do think it's good!
exercises.note: Wel contradicts the negative of the other person: niet goed against wel goed. English uses a stressed 'do' for this.

exercises.nl: Je hebt het ___ niet vergeten? We hadden om acht uur afgesproken.
exercises.en: You haven't forgotten, have you? We had agreed on eight o'clock.
exercises.note: Toch niet asks for reassurance: surely not? The speaker hopes the answer is no.

exercises.nl: Ik maak ___ een praatje met de buurvrouw, ik ben zo terug.
exercises.en: I'm just having a quick chat with the neighbour, I'll be right back.
exercises.note: Even says it will only take a moment. It stands after the verb and the subject, before the object.

exercises.nl: Hij zegt dat hij ziek is, maar dat zal ___ een smoes zijn.
exercises.en: He says he is ill, but that is probably an excuse.
exercises.note: Zal … wel is a guess: probably. Vast (surely), vast wel and waarschijnlijk give almost the same meaning and are also right.

exercises.nl: Vind jij dat niet beleefd? Ik vind het ___ beleefd.
exercises.en: Don't you think that's polite? I do think it's polite.
exercises.note: Wel is the opposite of niet: it contradicts the negative. English stresses 'do' instead.

exercises.en: No, don't worry, you're not disturbing me at all.
exercises.note: Nee hoor is a friendly no: no, don't worry. Hoor can stand straight after ja or nee. Nee joh, more familiar, is also right.

exercises.nl: Ik kreeg vandaag een compliment van mijn baas. — Waarvoor ___?
exercises.en: I got a compliment from my boss today. — What for, then?
exercises.note: Dan in a question reacts to what you have just heard and asks for more.

answers: Mag ik je even iets vragen?
exercises.note: The short pronoun je comes before the particle even. The rest follows, and the infinitive vragen goes to the end.

exercises.en: Better not do it after all.
exercises.note: The pronoun het comes first, then the particles in their fixed order, toch before maar, and niet after them.

exercises.task: Make the request friendlier with even.
exercises.en: Could you pass me the salt?
exercises.note: Even after the pronoun me. A noun with het or de may stand before or after even, so both orders are right.

exercises.task: Turn it into a question that expects 'yes', with toch.
exercises.from: Je vond het een leuk onderwerp.
answers: Je vond het toch een leuk onderwerp?
Je vond het een leuk onderwerp, toch?
exercises.en: You liked the topic, didn't you?
exercises.note: Toch asks for agreement. In the middle it comes after the pronoun het; it can also stand at the end after a comma.
Wel takes the place of niet and says the opposite. It is the Dutch answer to a negative.

exercises.wrong: Is dat niet een beetje brutaal, hoor?
answers: Is dat niet een beetje brutaal?
exercises.note: Hoor never goes in a question. It belongs at the end of a statement: Dat is een beetje brutaal, hoor.
A short pronoun such as het comes before the particle: Zeg het maar. A waiter uses the same words: What can I get you?
